about.dates: This report covers your session on Tuesday 18 August 2026 and was prepared on 18 August 2026. If a session is re-analysed, the report is prepared again and carries the new date.
about.footnote: Measured and prepared with PinPoint Studio. Swing images show only the golfer; video stays in the studio.
about.measured: 6 swings with a 7 iron, with every ball measured by a GC Quad.
about.notChecked: Some things could not be checked on every swing. When your hips turned fastest: the face-on camera cannot time a turn while you are square to it; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (6 of 6 swings). How fast the club was moving at its peak: our cameras could see it, but not well enough to judge (6 of 6 swings). Hip turn at the top: a single face-on camera cannot measure how far you turn; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (6 of 6 swings). Chest turn at the finish: a single face-on camera cannot measure how far you turn; a down-the-line camera or a body sensor can (6 of 6 swings). Nothing in this report depends on them.
about.ranges: Each habit is judged against a target range. Most ranges are coaching judgement, set from what good ball-strikers do; a few come from published measurements. They are not fitted to you. A swing outside the range is not a mistake in itself — it is where the evidence points. “Ruled out” on a work-on page means measured, and fine, on these swings with these cameras — not gone for good.

items: Your upper body leans toward the target at address
rows.title: Ruled out — measured, and fine

workOns.check: Film face-on. At the top your head and chest should sit a little behind the ball, never toward the target.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Reverse spine angle at P4, or “leaning left at the top”, “forward spine angle at the top”.
workOns.cue: At the top, feel your breastbone stay over your trail thigh.

drills.equipment: a mirror, or a phone on a stand
drills.instruction: Without a ball, hold a club across your chest. Turn to the top and check in a mirror, or on a phone face-on, that your head and chest sit a little behind the ball, with your upper body tilted slightly away from the target. Make ten slow turns.
drills.label: Club across the chest
drills.note: A short turn often hides inside this one: if the shoulders cannot turn further, the body tips instead, and a physical check of your upper back comes first.
drills.targets: To feel your upper body staying behind the ball as it turns, rather than tipping toward the target or hanging too far back.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: lean away from the target at the top, in degrees.
workOns.goal: Lean slightly away from the target at the top
workOns.kicker: Work-on 1 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  6 of 6 swings
workOns.name: Reverse spine angle at P4
workOns.saw: You lean toward the target at the top — on all 6 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical lean away from the target at the top: 5° the other way (you lean more toward the target at the top), against a target of 0° or more; this is mostly a small miss, but well past the range on 1 of 6 swings.
workOns.target: Lean away from the target at the top: 0° or more, on most swings. Today: 5° the other way (you lean more toward the target at the top).
workOns.why: Leaning toward the target at the top strains your lower back and makes it hard to start down smoothly.

workOns.cameWith: The coaching model says it can bring other habits with it. Not today — on every swing, your hips shift a little toward the target coming down, your weight moves onto your lead side through impact and the club bottoms out just past the ball.

workOns.check: Film face-on with a stick standing upright just outside your trail hip at address. At the top your hip should turn without pushing past it.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Sway, or “swaying off the ball”, “lateral slide back”.
workOns.cue: Feel your trail hip pocket turn behind you, as if your trail leg were a post you turn around.

drills.equipment: an alignment stick outside the trail hip, optional
drills.instruction: Take your address position, make a slow backswing turn, and stop at the top. Feel the pressure in the trail hip socket rather than on the outside of the trail foot. Hold for three seconds, then return.
drills.label: Trail hip load and hold
drills.note: The stick is a feedback aid, not the drill. If the hip cannot rotate internally, the slide is the body finding the only route it has.
drills.targets: To feel the trail hip accepting the turn instead of the pelvis sliding away from the target.

drills.instruction: Set up with your trail heel a few inches from a wall and make backswings without touching it.
drills.label: Trail heel against a wall
drills.note: Pairs with the hip load drill; this one gives the feedback, that one gives the feel.
drills.targets: To feel a backswing that turns rather than slides.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: hip movement away from the target going back, minus meaning toward it, in percent of stance width.
workOns.goal: Turn your hips in place going back
workOns.kicker: Work-on 2 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  6 of 6 swings
workOns.name: Sway
workOns.saw: Your hips sway away from the target going back — on all 6 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical hip movement away from the target going back, minus meaning toward it: 26% stance width, against a target of 20% stance width or less; this is a clear miss: well past the range on 3 of 6 swings.
workOns.target: Hip movement away from the target going back, minus meaning toward it: 20% stance width or less, on most swings. Today: 26% stance width.
workOns.why: When your hips slide away, the bottom of your swing moves and contact gets harder to repeat.

workOns.also: “cupped at the top”, “cupping at the top”
workOns.cameWith: The coaching model says it can bring other habits with it. Not today — on every swing, the club gets to about parallel at the top.

items:

A quick physical test would tell: Wrist mobility
rows.title: Could be behind it — we couldn't check

workOns.check: Film from down the line and pause at the top. The back of your lead wrist should look flat, in line with your forearm; a wrist bent back, with creases on the back of it, has cupped.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Lead wrist cupped at the top, or “cupped at the top”, “cupping at the top”.
workOns.cue: At the top, feel the back of your lead hand and your forearm make one flat surface, as if a ruler were laid along them.

drills.equipment: a playing card or a folded scorecard
drills.instruction: Slide a playing card or a folded scorecard under your glove strap or watch strap, flat against the back of your lead wrist. Make slow swings to the top and to impact, keeping the card lying flat: if it digs into your wrist, the wrist has cupped; if its end lifts away from your hand, the wrist has bowed.
drills.label: Card on the lead wrist
drills.note: The grip comes first: a grip turned well to one side sets the wrist cupped or bowed before the swing starts, and no wrist drill outlasts it. If the wrist cannot reach flat in slow motion, screen its mobility before repeating this.
drills.targets: To feel what a flat lead wrist is like at the top and into impact.

drills.equipment: a mirror or a phone on a stand
drills.instruction: Stand side-on to a mirror, or film from down the line. Swing slowly to the top and hold it for three seconds while you check the one thing your work-on names: the clubface, the lead wrist, where the shaft points or how far it has gone. Move into the position you want, feel it, then swing on from there and hit a gentle shot.
drills.label: Hold the top in the mirror
drills.note: A position held still is easier than one passed through at speed: once it feels normal held, test it in half swings before full ones. If you cannot reach the position even slowly, that is a mobility question before it is a practice one.
drills.targets: To learn what the position you want at the top feels like, by matching it to a picture of it.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: lead-wrist bow added by the top, in degrees.
workOns.goal: Set your lead wrist flat at the top
workOns.kicker: Work-on 3 of 5  ·  P4, at the top  ·  5 of 6 swings
workOns.name: Lead wrist cupped at the top
workOns.saw: Your lead wrist cups at the top — on 5 of 6 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical lead-wrist bow added by the top: 18° the other way (your lead wrist is more cupped at the top), against a target of −11° or more; this is a clear miss: well past the range on 5 of 6 swings.
workOns.target: Lead-wrist bow added by the top: −11° or more, on most swings. Today: 18° the other way (your lead wrist is more cupped at the top).
workOns.why: A cupped lead wrist opens the clubface, so you have more to square coming down or the ball slices.

rows.title: Ruled out — measured, and fine

workOns.check: Film face-on. Halfway down, your hands should still be in front of the middle of your chest, with your chest already turning toward the ball.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Arms outrun the chest, or “arms first”, “arms take over”.
workOns.cue: Feel your arms and the club stay in front of your chest as it turns, as if your chest were carrying them down.

drills.instruction: Tuck a small towel under your lead upper arm and make three-quarter swings without dropping it.
drills.label: Towel under the lead arm
drills.note: Easy to overdo. The arm should stay connected, not pinned — a swing with no separation at all is its own fault.
drills.targets: To feel the lead arm and the chest moving as one unit through the backswing.

drills.instruction: Make swings with a one-second pause at the top. From the pause, start down with your lower body, letting your weight move toward your lead foot while your chest stays behind the ball for a moment. Start with half swings and short irons.
drills.label: Pause at the top
drills.note: The pause is a rehearsal, not a new swing. Once the order feels natural, let the pause shrink until it has gone.
drills.targets: To give your lower body time to start the downswing, so your upper body is not rushed toward the ball.

workOns.goal: Turn your chest and let your arms follow
workOns.kicker: Work-on 4 of 5  ·  P7, at impact  ·  6 of 6 swings
workOns.name: Arms outrun the chest
workOns.saw: Your arms race ahead of your chest coming down — on all 6 swings, no change from first swing to last. Typical when your chest reached full speed: 10 ms before impact.
workOns.why: When your arms take over before your chest has turned, the speed your body made is left behind and your arms have to make it alone.

items: A quick physical test would tell: Balance on one leg
rows.title: Could be behind it — we couldn't check

items: Your feet are too close together
Your chest lunges toward the target coming down
You hang back on your trail side through impact
rows.title: Ruled out — measured, and fine

workOns.check: Film face-on and hold the finish until the ball lands. Your hips should be stacked over your lead foot, and you should be able to stand there without stepping.
workOns.coachTerm: Coaches call the habit Cannot hold the finish, or “falling over”, “stepping through”.
workOns.cue: Feel yourself swing to a tall finish with your weight on your lead heel and your trail toe just resting on the ground.

drills.instruction: Hit the shot and hold your finish, balanced on the lead foot, until the ball lands. If you cannot hold it, take 20 yards off the swing and try again.
drills.label: Hold the finish
drills.note: The most diagnostic drill in this list: where you fall tells you what happened earlier.
drills.targets: To make balance the constraint the swing is built inside, rather than something checked afterwards.

drills.instruction: Stand with your feet together and hit easy half to three-quarter shots off a low tee. Let your arms swing and your body turn only as fast as you can stay balanced, and hold the finish each time.
drills.label: Feet-together swings
drills.note: Short shots only. If you cannot stay balanced even at half speed, balance on one leg is worth checking before anything else.
drills.targets: To feel the arms, body and club working together at a speed your balance can support, rather than the body lunging or the arms going on their own.

workOns.figureLabel: Each dot is one swing: how far your hips finish from over your lead foot, in percent of stance width.
workOns.goal: Finish balanced over your lead foot
workOns.kicker: Work-on 5 of 5  ·  P10, at the finish  ·  5 of 6 swings
workOns.name: Cannot hold the finish
workOns.saw: You can't hold your finish — on 5 of 6 swings, easing as the session went on. Typical how far your hips finish from over your lead foot: 45% stance width, against a target of 35% stance width or less; this is a clear miss: well past the range on 3 of 6 swings.
workOns.target: How far your hips finish from over your lead foot: 35% stance width or less, on most swings. Today: 45% stance width.
workOns.why: A finish you can't hold shows your swing was off balance earlier, so your shots are hard to repeat.
